summary: An array keeps items of the same type in one block of memory so any item can be reached by its index.
key_points: Index starts at 0; Access by index is O(1); Insert or delete in the middle needs shifting
worked_example: In int a[5] the address of a[3] is the start address plus 3 times 4 bytes.
common_mistakes: Reading past the last index; Forgetting that the last index is n-1
practice_questions: Insert 7 at index 2 of an array of 5 numbers and show the shifting; Find a value with binary search in a sorted array

summary: A linked list stores data in nodes and each node points to the next node.
key_points: Head points to the first node; Insert at head is O(1); Access by position is O(n)
worked_example: To delete a middle node make the node before it point to the node after it and then free the removed node.
common_mistakes: Losing the head pointer; Forgetting to free a deleted node
practice_questions: Draw the list after inserting 10 then 20 then 30 at the tail; Delete the head node from a list of three nodes

summary: A stack adds and removes items only at the top so the newest item leaves first.
key_points: Push adds on top; Pop removes the top; Peek reads the top; Used for undo and function calls
worked_example: Push 1 then 2 then 3 and pop once and the top becomes 2.
common_mistakes: Popping from an empty stack; Mixing up LIFO with FIFO
practice_questions: Check the brackets in the text (a+b)*c using a stack; Evaluate the postfix expression 5 1 2 + 4 * +

summary: A queue adds items at the rear and removes them from the front so the oldest item leaves first.
key_points: Enqueue at rear; Dequeue from front; Circular queue reuses freed space with (index + 1) % size
worked_example: With size 5 and front at 3 and 3 items the rear sits at index 0 because the indexes wrap around.
common_mistakes: Letting rear run past the array end; Confusing full and empty states
practice_questions: Show front and rear after 4 enqueues and 2 dequeues in a size 5 circular queue; Explain why a simple array queue wastes space

summary: A hash table uses a hash function to turn a key into a bucket index for fast search.
key_points: Hash function key % size; Collision means two keys share a bucket; Chaining keeps a list in each bucket; Rehash when the table is too full
worked_example: With 11 buckets the keys 1001 and 1012 both give index 0 so they collide and are chained together.
common_mistakes: Using a bad hash function; Forgetting to rehash a crowded table
practice_questions: Insert 15 and 26 and 37 into a table of size 11 and list the buckets; Explain the load factor

summary: A binary search tree keeps smaller values in the left subtree and larger values in the right subtree.
key_points: Inorder traversal gives sorted order; Search is O(log n) on average; Sorted input makes it a skewed tree
worked_example: Insert 50 then 30 then 70 then 20 then 40 and the inorder output is 20 30 40 50 70.
common_mistakes: Forgetting the two-children delete case; Thinking the tree always stays balanced
practice_questions: Delete the root of a tree built from 50 30 70 20 40 60 80; List preorder and postorder for the same tree

summary: An AVL tree is a binary search tree that rebalances itself with rotations after every insert and delete.
key_points: Balance factor is left height minus right height; Allowed values are -1 and 0 and 1; Cases are LL and RR and LR and RL
worked_example: Insert 10 then 20 then 30 and the tree is right heavy so one left rotation makes 20 the root.
common_mistakes: Mixing up the LR and RL rotations; Not updating heights after a rotation
practice_questions: Insert 30 then 10 then 20 and name the rotation needed; Insert 1 to 7 in order and draw the final tree

summary: A max heap is a complete binary tree stored in an array where every parent is at least as large as its children.
key_points: Left child of i is 2i+1; Right child of i is 2i+2; Insert uses heapify up; Extract uses heapify down
worked_example: In the heap 50 30 40 10 20 extracting the max moves 20 to the root and heapify down gives 40 30 20 10.
common_mistakes: Using the wrong child index formula; Forgetting to heapify after extract
practice_questions: Insert 60 into the heap 50 30 40 10 20 and show the array; Build a max heap from 3 9 2 7 5

summary: A graph is a set of vertices joined by edges and a directed edge A to B shows that A comes before B.
key_points: Adjacency list uses O(V+E) space; BFS uses a queue; DFS uses a stack or recursion; A visited array stops endless loops
worked_example: For the edges 1 to 2 and 1 to 3 and 2 to 4 a BFS from 1 visits 1 then 2 then 3 then 4.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to mark vertices visited; Mixing directed and undirected edges
practice_questions: Write the adjacency list for a graph with 4 vertices and 4 edges; Run DFS from vertex 1 on that graph

summary: A class is a blueprint and an object is one real instance created from it.
key_points: Constructor runs on creation; Destructor starts with ~; this points to the current object; Static members are shared
worked_example: Student s1 creates an object and s1.name reads its member with the dot operator.
common_mistakes: Forgetting the semicolon after a class; Using the dot with a pointer instead of ->
practice_questions: Create a Book class with title and price and a constructor; Explain when a destructor runs

summary: Encapsulation keeps data private and gives access only through public methods.
key_points: private protected public; Getters read and setters write; Setters can validate
worked_example: A setAge function can reject negative ages so the object never holds a wrong value.
common_mistakes: Making every member public; Writing a setter with no validation
practice_questions: Write a BankAccount class where the balance cannot go negative; Explain protected with an example

summary: Abstraction shows what an object does and hides how it does it.
key_points: Pure virtual function = 0; Abstract class cannot be instantiated; Interface has only pure virtual functions
worked_example: A Shape class with a pure virtual area function forces Circle and Rectangle to write their own area.
common_mistakes: Trying to create an object of an abstract class; Forgetting to override every pure virtual function
practice_questions: Create an abstract Shape and two derived classes; Explain abstraction with a mobile phone example

summary: Inheritance lets a derived class reuse and extend the members of a base class.
key_points: Syntax class Dog : public Animal; Constructors run base first; Destructors run derived first; Diamond problem is solved with virtual inheritance
worked_example: Dog inherits eat from Animal and adds its own bark function.
common_mistakes: Expecting private base members in the derived class; Forgetting the base constructor call
practice_questions: Create Person then Student then GradStudent as a multilevel chain; Explain the diamond problem

summary: Polymorphism lets the same call behave differently depending on the object.
key_points: Overloading is compile time; Overriding with virtual is runtime; Use a base pointer to call derived code; override keyword checks mistakes
worked_example: A base pointer to a Dog object calls the Dog version of speak because speak is virtual.
common_mistakes: Forgetting virtual in the base class; Thinking return type alone can overload a function
practice_questions: Overload an add function for int and double; Show runtime polymorphism with Animal and Dog

summary: The relational model stores data in tables and uses keys to identify and link rows.
key_points: Primary key is unique and not null; Foreign key points to another table; Candidate key is a minimal unique set
worked_example: Enrollment holds StudentID as a foreign key that must exist in the Student table.
common_mistakes: Using a changing value as a primary key; Allowing a foreign key with no matching row
practice_questions: List the candidate keys of a Student table; Explain referential integrity with an example

summary: An ER diagram shows entities and their attributes and how they relate.
key_points: Rectangle entity; Oval attribute; Diamond relationship; Many-to-many needs a junction table
worked_example: Students and Courses are many-to-many so we create an Enrollment table with both keys.
common_mistakes: Drawing attributes as entities; Forgetting cardinality
practice_questions: Draw an ER diagram for a library with books and members; Convert a many-to-many relationship into tables

summary: SQL is used to create tables and to insert and read and change and delete data.
key_points: DDL is CREATE and ALTER and DROP; DML is SELECT and INSERT and UPDATE and DELETE; WHERE filters rows
worked_example: SELECT name FROM Student WHERE marks > 80 returns the names of high scoring students.
common_mistakes: Running UPDATE or DELETE without WHERE; Mixing up DELETE and DROP
practice_questions: Write a query to list students ordered by marks; Write a query that counts students per department

summary: A join combines rows from two tables using a related column.
key_points: INNER keeps matches only; LEFT keeps all left rows; CROSS gives every combination; Aggregates are SUM AVG MIN MAX COUNT
worked_example: A LEFT JOIN from Student to Result shows students with no result as NULL.
common_mistakes: Forgetting the ON condition; Using WHERE instead of HAVING for groups
practice_questions: Join Student and Department to show the department name; Write a query using a subquery

summary: Normalization splits tables so each fact is stored once and anomalies disappear.
key_points: 1NF atomic values; 2NF no partial dependency; 3NF no transitive dependency; BCNF is stricter
worked_example: A cell with two phone numbers breaks 1NF so we put each number in its own row.
common_mistakes: Checking 2NF when the key is not composite; Splitting tables without a lossless join
practice_questions: Normalize a table holding order and customer and product columns to 3NF; Find the functional dependencies in a given table

summary: A transaction is a group of operations that must succeed or fail together.
key_points: Atomicity and Consistency and Isolation and Durability; COMMIT saves; ROLLBACK undoes; Locks control concurrency
worked_example: In a bank transfer the debit and the credit must both happen or neither happens.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to commit; Confusing isolation with durability
practice_questions: Explain each ACID property with a bank example; Describe a dirty read and how isolation prevents it

summary: A process is a running program and a thread is a lightweight path of execution inside it.
key_points: Process states are new ready running waiting terminated; Threads share code and data; Each thread has its own stack; Context switch saves and loads state
worked_example: A browser can run each tab as a process and use threads inside a tab for loading and drawing.
common_mistakes: Thinking threads have separate heaps; Mixing up Ready and Waiting
practice_questions: Draw the process state diagram; Compare a process and a thread in a table

summary: The scheduler picks the next ready process using rules such as FCFS or SJF or Round Robin.
key_points: FCFS can cause the convoy effect; SJF minimizes average waiting time; Round Robin uses a time quantum; Aging prevents starvation
worked_example: With bursts 4 and 3 under FCFS the second process waits 4 units.
common_mistakes: Mixing up waiting time and turnaround time; Forgetting arrival times
practice_questions: Find the average waiting time for bursts 5 and 3 and 2 under FCFS and SJF; Run Round Robin with quantum 2

summary: Synchronization makes sure processes use shared data one at a time in the right order.
key_points: Race condition; Critical section; Mutex and semaphore; Producer consumer problem
worked_example: Two processes adding to one counter can lose an update unless a mutex protects the addition.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to release a lock; Using busy waiting everywhere
practice_questions: Explain the producer consumer problem with a semaphore; List the three requirements of a critical section solution

summary: A deadlock happens when processes hold resources and wait in a circle for more.
key_points: Four Coffman conditions; Prevention avoidance detection recovery; Banker's algorithm; Safe state
worked_example: P1 holds R1 and wants R2 while P2 holds R2 and wants R1 which makes a circular wait.
common_mistakes: Confusing deadlock with starvation; Saying an unsafe state is always a deadlock
practice_questions: List the four conditions for a deadlock; Explain how ordering resources stops circular wait

summary: Memory management decides where each process lives in main memory.
key_points: Paging uses fixed pages; Segmentation uses variable parts; Internal and external fragmentation; First fit and best fit and worst fit
worked_example: With 1 KB pages the logical address 3000 is in page 2 at offset 952.
common_mistakes: Mixing up internal and external fragmentation; Forgetting the page offset
practice_questions: Place processes of 212 and 417 and 112 using first fit and best fit; Calculate page number and offset for address 5000 with 1 KB pages

summary: Virtual memory lets a program run even when only some of its pages are in RAM.
key_points: Demand paging; Page fault; FIFO and LRU and Optimal replacement; Thrashing
worked_example: For the reference string 1 2 3 1 with 3 frames FIFO gives 3 page faults.
common_mistakes: Counting hits as faults; Ignoring Belady's anomaly
practice_questions: Count page faults for 7 0 1 2 0 3 0 4 with 3 frames using FIFO and LRU; Explain thrashing

summary: A file system organizes files and directories on a disk.
key_points: Contiguous and linked and indexed allocation; inode holds metadata; Permissions rwx; Journaling helps recovery
worked_example: Linked allocation stores a pointer to the next block in every block which makes random access slow.
common_mistakes: Confusing hard and soft links; Forgetting external fragmentation in contiguous allocation
practice_questions: Compare the three allocation methods in a table; Explain absolute and relative paths

summary: A variable is a named place in memory and its data type decides what it can hold.
key_points: int and double and char and bool; const makes a value fixed; Integer division drops the decimal part
worked_example: int x = 5 and then 5 / 2 gives 2 because both numbers are integers.
common_mistakes: Using a variable before giving it a value; Dividing two integers and expecting decimals
practice_questions: Declare variables for name initial age and gpa; Print the result of 7 / 2 and 7.0 / 2

summary: Operators combine values to calculate results or to compare and join conditions.
key_points: Arithmetic and comparison and logical operators; Precedence decides the order; x++ uses the value then adds one
worked_example: 2 + 3 * 4 is 14 because multiplication happens before addition.
common_mistakes: Writing = instead of ==; Forgetting operator precedence
practice_questions: Evaluate 10 - 4 / 2 + 3; Write a condition that checks a number is even and positive

summary: Conditional statements run different code depending on whether a condition is true.
key_points: if and else if and else; switch with case and break; 0 is false and any other number is true
worked_example: A grade program checks 80 and above first then 60 and above and the first true condition wins.
common_mistakes: Missing break in a switch; Writing = inside an if condition
practice_questions: Write a program that prints Pass or Fail from marks; Write a switch for the days of the week

summary: A loop repeats a block of code until its condition becomes false.
key_points: for when the count is known; while checks first; do-while runs at least once; break and continue
worked_example: A loop from 1 to 5 adding each number gives the sum 15.
common_mistakes: Off-by-one mistakes; A condition that never becomes false
practice_questions: Print the table of 7 up to 10 times; Print a right triangle of stars with nested loops

summary: A function packs a task into a named block that can be called many times.
key_points: Return type and parameters; Pass by value copies and pass by reference changes the original; Recursion needs a base case
worked_example: factorial(4) calls factorial(3) and so on until the base case factorial(0) returns 1 and the answer is 24.
common_mistakes: Forgetting the return statement; A recursive function with no base case
practice_questions: Write a function that returns the larger of two numbers; Write a recursive function for the sum of 1 to n

summary: An array holds many values of one type and a string holds a sequence of characters.
key_points: Index starts at 0; Out of range access is undefined; std::string has length and + and ==; getline reads a full line
worked_example: To sum an array of size n loop with i from 0 to n-1 and add each element.
common_mistakes: Going past the last index; Using cin when a full line with spaces is needed
practice_questions: Find the largest value in an array of 10 numbers; Count the vowels in a string

summary: A pointer stores the address of another variable and a reference is another name for a variable.
key_points: & gives the address and * reaches the value; new allocates and delete frees; nullptr points to nothing; A reference cannot be null
worked_example: After int *p = &x then *p = 9 changes x to 9.
common_mistakes: Forgetting delete after new; Using a pointer after it was freed
practice_questions: Swap two numbers using pointers; Allocate an array with new and free it with delete[]
